description: A team of two highly motiviated University students who are obsessed with the field of aerospace.
summary:
A moon lander ideally wants to land in an area with two things: sunlight for power, and a line of sight to the Earth for radio. Both of these factors depend heavily on the terrain

We created a tool that uses an interactive 3D map to allow users to select a landing point on the moon. This tool uses existing NASA data and works out the skyline from the terrain and checks hour by hour over a year, whether the Sun and Earth are above it.  The tool reports how long the Earth is visible, how long the Sun is visible, and how long both are visible together. It also repots the longest night, the power available, and ranks the candidate sites.

Our results show a ridge near Shackleton crater in sunlight 88.5% of the year, against about 48% at the Apollo 11 site, and a nearby mountain that never loses sight of Earth.
details:
Our tool allows a user to select any point on an interactive 3D Moon as a landing site, and analyses that site. The Moon can be coloured by sunlight, Earth visibility, or longest night, so the user can see promising regions before choosing a point. In the analysis, our tool uses LOLA terrain data from the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter to compute a skyline: for each direction around the point, it finds how high the terrain rises above the horizon. It then uses Sun and Earth positions from JPL Horizons to show their paths against this skyline, and checks hour by hour through 2027 whether each is above or below it. Our analysis shows the percentage of the year with sunlight, the percentage with the Earth in view, the percentage with both, the longest night, the longest radio gap, and the solar panel power. Our dashboard compares landing sites side by side, scores them with a 40% weight on sunlight, 30% on Earth visibility and 30% on safe ground, and recommends one.

The site runs in the browser with no installation. Any clicked point is estimated on the spot from precomputed terrain, and candidate sites are analysed in full detail in advance. Apollo and IM-2 landing sites are also marked for reference.

Our tool provides many benefits to enthusiasts and scientists. Checking how much sunlight and earth visibility a lunar site gets normally means downloading large terrain files and writing code to process them. Our tool allows users to do this in one click, with the answer appearing in seconds. On the other hand, users are not limited to a fixed list of sites. any point on the moon can be analyzed and compared with others. The tool allows users to watch the sun dip behind a crater rim, which a single number cannot show. Often, mission planners will have to face choosing between various factors such as better power or better communication. Our comparison table allows users to visibly see these trade-offs.

We intended this as a first-look screening tool. Small teams such as university groups, student rover projects and startups could use it to narrow down candidate sites before investing in detailed studies. This tool is also great for education, showing students and the public why the Moon's south pole matters and why landing there is difficult using real data.

This tool makes it easier to understand NASA's existing data. While LOLA terrain grids and JPL Horizons are public, they are hard to use without programming experience. Our tool puts the data behind a simple interface.

Our team has put a lot of thought behind this and implemented our ideas in creative ways. Instead of having a database where it was easier to read or only having a 2D page, our team went with a 3D Moon because it felt more true to the nature of what we intend the tool to be used for. Being avid players of games like Kerbal Space Program, we wanted to recreate the feeling with this project. Planning is a very important step of every mission, and it is more important than ever that planners get the full picture.

We recognize that our project has not reached the full potential of what it can do as of yet, and therefore have some next steps planned for the future. these include:

- A longer time span. Our data covers every hour of 2027, which is one full lunar season. The exact lighting pattern shifts slightly each year and only repeats every 18.6 years, as the Moon’s orbit slowly wobbles. Running the full cycle would find the sites that stay well lit every year, and the true worst-case night at each one.

- Finer terrain beyond the pole. Outside the south polar region we use a grid with one height every 1.9 km, which misses small hills and crater walls. Using higher-resolution LOLA grids there would make the whole-Moon results as reliable as the polar ones, and would let us give the north pole the same detailed treatment.

- Model the lander, not just the site. Adding spacecraft details such as solar panel size, battery capacity and antenna height would turn the results into mission answers: how big a battery this site needs to survive its longest night, or whether a taller mast would keep Earth in view.

- More of what a mission looks for. Sunlight and communication are only part of site selection. We would add permanently shadowed regions, where water ice may be found, and surface temperature, so users can find sites that are well lit but close to resources.

We used several programming languages and libraries to assist in the creation of this tool. Here is a list of what we used:

Languages:

- Python for the data pipeline. Downloading NASA data, computing skylines, sunlight, Earth visibility, power, slope, and scores

- JavaScript, HTML, and CSS for the website: the 3D map, the dashboard, and the start page

Libraries:

- NumPy for the terrain and geometry calculations

- Requests for downloading data from NASA services

- Matplotlib for the ground-slope pictures

- three.js for the interactive 3D Moon

- Plotly for the skyline and timeline charts

NASA data and services:

- LOLA elevation grids (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter) for terrain: 20 m and 120 m grids at the south pole, and the whole-Moon grid.

- JPL Horizons API for hourly sun and Earth positions in 2027

- LROC for the coordinates of the Apollo and IM-2 landing sites

Finally, our site is hosted and published on GitHub and GitHub Pages.

AI assistance (Claude) was used to help write and debug code. We chose the approach, ran the pipeline on NASA data ourselves, and checked the results.
